en: The Sutra on the Profound Kindness of Parents Spoken by the Buddha.

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas and their retinues, as well as bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Nuns, laymen, and laywomen,
as well as all the devas, humans, and celestial beings— nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas—
all came together for this assembly.
With single-minded devotion, they listened to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma,
gazing up at his venerable countenance without averting their eyes for even a moment.
The Buddha said:
"When a person is born into this world,
their parents are their kin."
It is not that one is not born without a father,
nor is one not nurtured without a mother.
Therefore, one is entrusted to the mother's womb and carries the body for ten months.
When the years were complete and the months fulfilled,
both mother and child manifested; she was born falling upon the grass,
where her parents raised her.
When lying down, he rests in a fragrant carriage;
when held in his parents' embrace,
he makes harmonious and playful sounds.
She smiled without speaking.
When hungry, one must eat;
it is not without a mother that one is fed.
When one is thirsty, one must drink;
it is not the mother who does not provide milk.
Among mothers, when hungry, she swallows what is bitter and spits out what is sweet, pushing away the dry and moving toward the moist.
One does not associate with those who act against what is right.
No one nurtures more than a mother;
a compassionate mother nurtures her child.
Setting aside the *lañchana*,
within the ten fingernails there is the impurity of the food consumed;
each should measure eight *hu* and four *dou*.
When one calculates and deliberates upon the kindness of one's mother, it is as vast as the great heavens and has no limit.
Alas! How can one ever repay such a compassionate mother?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One, how may one repay his kindness?
I only pray that you will explain this to me."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively and reflect upon it well;
I shall analyze and explain it for you."
The kindness of one's parents is as vast as heaven and has no limit.
How much more so for a filial and compassionate son who is able to create merit and produce scriptures on behalf of his parents?
Alternatively, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one may prepare a *pātra* and *urunda-bhājana* for the Buddha.
By offering these to the Buddha and the Sangha, one attains immeasurable fruits and is able to repay the kindness of one's parents.
If there should be another person who copies this sutra and disseminates it among the people of the world.
One who receives, maintains, reads,
and recites [this teaching] should be known as one who repays the kindness of their parents.
How can the kindness of parents be repaid?
However, as for his parents’ concerns regarding his comings and goings,
he frequently failed to return home at the proper times, leaving the neighbors to the east and west to worry about his well, hearth, mortar, and millstones.
"My son was weeping at home;
remembering me, he has come back immediately.
Seeing me from afar, the son [rejoiced].
Some ride in litters,
shaking their heads and wagging their tails;
others trail their bellies along as they walk.
Alas, mother! For the sake of her child, the mother bends her body down low;
she stretches out both hands and brushes away the dust.
She hummed softly, opened her heart, and let forth milk;
she gave the milk to him,
and the mother rejoiced upon seeing her child.
The child sees his mother and rejoices;
their two hearts are filled with affection, sorrow, and kinship—
a weight of compassion so profound it cannot be surpassed.
At two or three years of age, they begin to act with playful intent;
at mealtime, they do not know their father unless it is their mother who is unaware of him.
When the mother comes and goes, she encounters other seating arrangements.
Or, having obtained cakes or meat,
he would not eat them but would set aside the flavors,
carrying them back home to give them to his children.
Out of ten attempts, nine will succeed, and one will always bring constant joy;
yet if once it fails, one should not act with arrogance or weep feigningly.
A son who acts with such arrogance is unfilial.
There must be five types of grief;
the filial son does not harbor them.
There must be kindness and obedience.
Eventually, he grew up;
accompanied by his friends,
he combed and rubbed his hair.
Desiring fine garments to cover the body,
[he finds] his clothes worn out and tattered.
The parents themselves put on new and fine cotton silks,
first giving them to their child;
even when traveling or going about, they do so.
In matters of public or private urgency,
they turn their hearts toward the south and north;
in pursuit of their children, they follow them to the east and west.
He threw her head over the side.
Having sought a wife but instead obtained another's child,
his parents became increasingly estranged from him.
We take pleasure in conversing together within our private chambers;
yet our parents, advanced in years and with failing strength,
do not come to inquire after us from morning until evening.
Furthermore, her father was deceased and her mother was widowed;
she dwelt alone in an empty room,
like a traveler.
Dwelling in the houses of others,
he is always without affection or attachment;
furthermore, he is not affected by the cold.
They encounter bitter suffering and calamities;
they are extremely old with their appearance having faded,
and they abound with lice and nits.
Night and day he did not lie down,
sighing and heaving long-drawn breaths:
"What crime or past transgression has produced such an unfilial son?"
At times he would shout out,
glaring with eyes wide in rage and indignation,
returning to his son and reviling him.
With head bowed and a smile on his face, the wife was likewise unfilial; the son was likewise unfilial.
Furthermore, the five members of the household—husband and wife together—committed the five heinous crimes.
At that time, when summoned and ordered to act with haste,
nine out of ten times they disobeyed.
I will not comply at all;
I shall revile and harbor anger,
rather than die early.
When the parents heard this, they wept bitterly and were filled with grief and distress.
Tears flowed down both cheeks;
her eyes were swollen from weeping.
"When you were first born, it was not I who did not raise you."
"But my giving birth to you is not as good as original non-existence.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
If a son or daughter of good family can,

for the sake of their parents, receive, uphold, read, recite, or transcribe even a single phrase or a single verse of this Mahāyāna Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra on the Profound Kindness and Greatness of Parents.
All those who follow this single path shall have their five grave offenses of immediate retribution completely extinguished,
forever exhausted without remainder;
they shall always behold the Buddhas and hear the Dharma.
They will swiftly attain liberation.
Ānanda rose from his seat,
bared his right shoulder, and [prostrated].
Kneeling with palms joined,
he came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what is the name of this sutra?"
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"This sutra is named the Sutra on the Profound Weight of Parental Kindness."
If there are any sentient beings who,
for the sake of their parents, perform meritorious deeds, produce scriptures, burn incense, invite the Buddha, prostrate, and make offerings to the Triple Gem,
or provide food and drink to the Sangha;
One should know that such a person is able to repay the kindness of their parents.
When Śakra, Brahmā, the various devas, human beings, and all sentient beings hear this sutra,
they rejoice and resolve to attain the bodhicitta.
His wailing shook the earth;
tears fell like rain as he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground,
receiving the teaching with faith and bowing at the Buddha’s feet.
Rejoicing, they received and practiced it.
Thus concludes the *Sūtra on the Profound Kindness of Parents* spoken by the Buddha.
